section.title: Jeremiah Imprisoned
section.sectionRationale: Zedekiah is a weak king caught between fearing Babylon and fearing his own officials, and he privately wants Jeremiah's word even while publicly letting his officials abuse the prophet. Jeremiah is arrested as a deserter, beaten, and lowered into a muddy cistern to die, then rescued by an unlikely foreigner. Through it all he keeps repeating the one message the king cannot bring himself to obey: surrender to Babylon and live.
section.thesis: A king who wants a comforting word but will not obey the true one leaves his faithful prophet beaten, imprisoned, and sinking in the mud, yet God preserves Jeremiah through an outsider's courage and keeps offering Zedekiah life if only he will surrender, right up to the last possible moment.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: Zedekiah's fragile reign and Jeremiah's warning during a brief lull in the siege; Jeremiah arrested at the city gate and thrown into prison as a deserter; Jeremiah lowered into a cistern to die and rescued by Ebed-melech the Cushite; and a secret royal audience in which Zedekiah hears the truth yet cannot bring himself to act on it.

units.label: Zedekiah's fragile reign and Jeremiah's warning
units.note: a false lull in the siege

verses.text: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made Zedekiah son of Josiah the king of Judah, and he reigned in place of Coniah son of Jehoiakim.
But he and his officers and the people of the land refused to obey the words that the LORD had spoken through Jeremiah the prophet.
Yet King Zedekiah sent Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet with the message, “Please pray to the LORD our God for us!”
Now Jeremiah was free to come and go among the people, for they had not yet put him in prison.
Pharaoh's army had left Egypt, and when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard the report, they withdrew from Jerusalem.
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet:

“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says that you are to tell the king of Judah, who sent you to Me: Behold, Pharaoh's army, which has marched out to help you, will go back to its own land of Egypt.
Then the Chaldeans will return and fight against this city. They will capture it and burn it down.
This is what the LORD says: Do not deceive yourselves by saying, ‘The Chaldeans will go away for good,’ for they will not!
Indeed, if you were to strike down the entire army of the Chaldeans that is fighting against you, and only wounded men remained in their tents, they would still get up and burn this city down.”

units.label: Jeremiah arrested as a deserter
units.note: beaten and jailed on a false charge

verses.text: When the Chaldean army withdrew from Jerusalem for fear of Pharaoh's army,
Jeremiah started to leave Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to claim his portion there among the people.
But when he reached the Gate of Benjamin, the captain of the guard, whose name was Irijah son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah, seized him and said, “You are deserting to the Chaldeans!”

“That is a lie,” Jeremiah replied. “I am not deserting to the Chaldeans!” 
But Irijah would not listen to him; instead, he arrested Jeremiah and took him to the officials.
The officials were angry with Jeremiah, and they beat him and placed him in jail in the house of Jonathan the scribe, for it had been made into a prison.
So Jeremiah went into a cell in the dungeon and remained there a long time.

Later, King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah and received him in his palace, where he asked him privately, “Is there a word from the LORD?” 
“There is,” Jeremiah replied. “You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.”
Then Jeremiah asked King Zedekiah, “How have I sinned against you or your servants or these people, that you have put me in prison?
Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, claiming, ‘The king of Babylon will not come against you or this land’?
But now please listen, O my lord the king. May my petition come before you. Do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, or I will die there.”

So King Zedekiah gave orders for Jeremiah to be placed in the courtyard of the guard and given a loaf of bread daily from the street of the bakers, until all the bread in the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard.

units.label: Thrown into the cistern, rescued by Ebed-melech
units.note: sunk in the mud, lifted out by a foreigner

verses.text: Now Shephatiah son of Mattan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jucal son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur son of Malchijah heard that Jeremiah had been telling all the people:

“This is what the LORD says: Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine and plague, but whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live; he will retain his life like a spoil of war, and he will live.
This is what the LORD says: This city will surely be delivered into the hands of the army of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it.”

Then the officials said to the king, “This man ought to die, for he is discouraging the warriors who remain in this city, as well as all the people, by speaking such words to them; this man is not seeking the well-being of these people, but their ruin.”
“Here he is,” replied King Zedekiah. “He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you.”

So they took Jeremiah and dropped him into the {{bor|cistern}} of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the courtyard of the guard. They lowered Jeremiah with ropes into the cistern, which had no water but only mud, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud.
Now {{ebedmelech|Ebed-melech}} the Cushite, a court official in the royal palace, heard that Jeremiah had been put into the cistern. While the king was sitting at the Gate of Benjamin,
Ebed-melech went out from the king's palace and said to the king,

“My lord the king, these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet. They have dropped him into the cistern, where he will starve to death, for there is no more bread in the city.”
So the king commanded Ebed-melech the Cushite, “Take thirty men from here with you and pull Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies.”

Then Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the king's palace, to a place below the storehouse. From there he took old rags and worn-out clothes and lowered them with ropes to Jeremiah in the cistern.
Ebed-melech the Cushite cried out to Jeremiah, “Put these worn-out rags and clothes under your arms to pad the ropes.” Jeremiah did so,
and they pulled him up with the ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard.

units.label: A secret meeting, and Jeremiah's silence kept
units.note: the truth offered again, and refused

verses.text: Then King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance to the house of the LORD. “I am going to ask you something,” said the king to Jeremiah. “Do not hide anything from me.”
“If I tell you,” Jeremiah replied, “you will surely put me to death. And even if I give you advice, you will not listen to me.”

But King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has given us this life, I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.”

Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “This is what the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘If you indeed surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, then you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive.

But if you do not surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, then this city will be delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans. They will burn it down, and you yourself will not escape their grasp.’”
But King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, “I am afraid of the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans, for the Chaldeans may deliver me into their hands to abuse me.”
“They will not hand you over,” Jeremiah replied. “Obey the voice of the LORD in what I am telling you, that it may go well with you and you may live.
But if you refuse to surrender, this is the word that the LORD has shown me:

All the women who remain in the palace of the king of Judah will be brought out to the officials of the king of Babylon, and those women will say: 
‘They misled you and overcame you, those trusted friends of yours. Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.’
All your wives and children will be brought out to the Chaldeans. And you yourself will not escape their grasp, for you will be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city will be burned down.”
Then Zedekiah warned Jeremiah, “Do not let anyone know about this conversation, or you will die.
If the officials hear that I have spoken with you, and they come and demand of you, ‘Tell us what you said to the king and what he said to you; do not hide it from us, or we will kill you,’
then tell them, ‘I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there.’”

When all the officials came to Jeremiah and questioned him, he relayed to them the exact words the king had commanded him to say. So they said no more to him, for no one had overheard the conversation.
And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured.

bor.gloss: A pit or cistern, ordinarily dug to store rainwater. This one held only mud, and the officials intend it as a slow, deniable execution, since Jeremiah would starve or suffocate rather than be visibly killed.

ebedmelech.gloss: Literally servant of the king, likely a title or throne name rather than a birth name. A foreign court official, a Cushite, bears this name and becomes the one man in the palace who acts to save God's true prophet from the men who serve the king in name only.

basic.context: Zedekiah is Babylon's puppet king, caught between officials who want to fight and a prophet who keeps saying surrender is the only way to live. When Egypt's army briefly draws the Chaldeans away from the siege, Jeremiah tries to leave the city on personal business and is arrested as a deserter, beaten, and jailed. Later, when he keeps telling the people to surrender, the officials lower him into a muddy cistern to die quietly, and only the courage of Ebed-melech, a foreign court official, saves his life. Zedekiah keeps summoning Jeremiah secretly for the truth, and keeps being too afraid of his own officials to act on it.
basic.hermeneutics: Read as history, this narrative shows exactly how a nation destroys its own last chance: not through ignorance, since Zedekiah hears the true word repeatedly and privately believes enough of it to protect Jeremiah's life, but through fear of other people's opinion overriding fear of God. The rescue by Ebed-melech, an outsider with no political stake in the outcome, is a deliberate contrast to the insiders who either persecute the prophet or, like the king, know the truth and still will not act on it.
basic.originalLanguages: Jeremiah is thrown into a bor, a cistern meant for water but here holding only mud, a slow and deniable death sentence. His rescuer bears the name Ebed-melech, servant of the king, and it is this servant, not the king himself, who acts with the courage the name implies, exposing how far the actual court had drifted from true service to either God or king.
basic.typology: The righteous prophet sunk in the mire of a pit, rescued only by an outsider's intervention, echoes Joseph thrown into a pit by his brothers and points forward to Christ, the greater righteous sufferer cast down by His own people and vindicated by God.
basic.christ: Jeremiah's descent into mud, left to die quietly rather than executed openly, and his rescue by an unlikely foreigner, prefigure the pattern fulfilled in Christ: the true word of God, hated by the very people it was sent to save, brought low, yet preserved and vindicated by God's own hand, with grace reaching even those outside the covenant people, as it reached Ebed-melech.
basic.god: God preserves His prophet's life through the most unlikely instrument in the palace, showing His providence is not limited to Israel's own officials or even its king. At the same time, God continues offering Zedekiah a genuine way to survive, right up to the last private audience, showing His patience keeps extending even to a king who has already shown he lacks the courage to obey.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 37:24 has Joseph's brothers throw him into an empty pit before selling him. Psalm 40:2 pictures being lifted out of a miry pit and set on a rock, the very rescue Jeremiah experiences. Acts 16 shows God preserving His servants through prison in a way that still accomplishes His purposes. Hebrews 11:36-38 lists prophets who suffered chains and imprisonment for their faithfulness.
basic.oneStory: A faithful prophet is beaten and left to die in the mud for telling the truth, yet God preserves him through an outsider's courage while a fearful king forfeits his last chance at life. This is the recurring shape of the whole Bible: the true word of God suffers at the hands of those it came to save, yet is never finally destroyed, a pattern completed in Christ, the greater prophet rejected, buried, and raised.

context.literary:
Chapters 37 and 38 tell much the same story twice, and the doubling is the point. In each cycle Jeremiah is seized by hostile officials (37:13-15 and 38:1-6), kept in a place where he may die, then fetched by a wavering king for a private audience (37:17 and 38:14), and in each audience he ends by pleading not to be sent back to die (37:20 and 38:26). Both cycles close with the same sentence, that Jeremiah 'remained in the courtyard of the guard,' 37:21, 38:13 and 38:28. The repetition shows a king who is offered the truth again and again and keeps handing it back.

The sections are held together by a narrator who does not intrude, except twice. Verse 37:4 pauses to remark that Jeremiah was still free to come and go because 'they had not yet put him in prison,' a calm note that makes the reader brace for what follows. Then 38:28 ends on a simple date: he stayed there until the day the city was taken. In between, nearly everything is dialogue, and the dialogue is where the characters are drawn. Zedekiah speaks in questions and fears: 'Is there a word from the LORD?' 37:17; 'I am afraid of the Jews who have deserted,' 38:19. The officials speak in accusations. Jeremiah speaks in the plain word of the LORD, and then, once, in a request for mercy.

The hand is a recurring image. Jeremiah is 'in your hands' for the officials, 38:5, and the king keeps promising not to hand him over to 'these men,' 38:16, while the message to the king is that he will be delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans, 38:3, 38:18 and 38:19. Everyone in the story is in someone else's hand, and the question is whose hand holds the king.

The rescue scene stands out for its tenderness of detail. Ebed-melech takes ropes and old rags from a storeroom and tells Jeremiah to put them under his arms so that the ropes will not cut him, 38:11-12. After pages of speeches, the narrative slows down for a small act of kindness. Near the end, a short poem appears in 38:22, a taunt the king's own women will chant, the only poetry in the section, placed like a last warning at the point of the king's refusal.
context.historical:
Zedekiah was a puppet. Nebuchadnezzar made him king in 597 BC in place of his nephew Jehoiachin, who had been taken to Babylon, and changed his name, 2 Kings 24:17. Zedekiah swore an oath of loyalty in God's name, which he then broke by seeking help from Egypt, 2 Chronicles 36:13 and Ezekiel 17:13-16. 2 Chronicles 36:12 sums him up: he 'did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet.' The siege that began in his ninth year lasted until the city was breached in his eleventh, Jeremiah 52:4-7.

The pause in 37:5 is a real event. Pharaoh Hophra, called Apries by the Greeks, moved an Egyptian force toward Judah, and the Babylonians lifted the siege to meet it. Jeremiah 34:21-22 anticipates the moment and announces that the Babylonians will come back. For a few days Jerusalem believed it was saved, and Jeremiah's task was to tell them they were not. He tried to leave at that moment, and the arrest at the Gate of Benjamin, a northern gate toward the territory of Benjamin where his hometown of Anathoth lay, shows how charged the moment was. The charge of desertion was plausible. People were going over to the Babylonians, and Zedekiah himself fears them, 38:19.

Ancient letters give a feeling for the time. The Lachish ostraca, written on potsherds by a military commander to his superior during these months, speak of watching for signals and of fortresses falling. One of the letters complains of officials whose words 'weaken the hands' of the people, which is the same expression behind 'discouraging' in 38:4. It is likely that this was the ordinary charge laid against anyone who urged surrender. Clay seal impressions published from excavations in Jerusalem's City of David bear names matching Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur, two of the officials named in 38:1.

The places are exact. A scribe's house, Jonathan's, had been turned into a prison, 37:15, and the courtyard of the guard was in the royal palace compound, 32:2. Cisterns were common in Jerusalem, plastered chambers cut in rock to hold rainwater, with a narrow neck at the top. By late in a siege, with no bread left in the city, 38:9, such a cistern could be dry but for a layer of mud, and a man lowered in by ropes would not be able to climb out. Ebed-melech was a Cushite, from Nubia on the upper Nile, one of the Africans who served in Judah's court. The Hebrew term for his office can mean eunuch or official.
context.canonical:
Jeremiah's suffering is a thread through the book. Pashhur son of Immer had him beaten and put in the stocks, 20:1-2, and he was nearly put to death for his words about the temple in chapter 26. In 11:19 he had said he was like a gentle lamb led to slaughter, someone to be cut off from the land of the living. The cistern is the sharpest point of that history, and when the Lamentations poet speaks of being thrown alive into a pit with waters closing over his head, 3:53-55, readers have long heard Jeremiah's voice in it, whether or not he is the author.

The pit and the mud draw on the Psalms. Psalm 69:2 says, 'I have sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing,' and Psalm 69:14 prays, 'Rescue me from the mire and do not let me sink.' Psalm 40:2 recalls the answer: 'He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay.' The Hebrew of these verses and of Jeremiah 38 share the nouns and verbs of the pit, the mire, sinking and lifting. Genesis 37:24 is the oldest pit in Scripture, where Joseph is thrown by his brothers.

Other prophets met prison for the same offence. Micaiah son of Imlah was put in prison on bread and water for telling a king the truth, 1 Kings 22:26-27, and Hanani the seer was jailed by Asa, 2 Chronicles 16:10. Zedekiah's first request, 'Please pray to the LORD our God for us,' 37:3, recalls the earlier one in 21:1-2, where the same Pashhur son of Malchijah came on his behalf, hoping the LORD would work a wonder.

The foreigner who does right when Israel's own do wrong is another biblical pattern. Cush stretches out her hands to God in Psalm 68:31, and Zephaniah 3:10 has worshippers coming from beyond the rivers of Cush. Isaiah 56:3-5 promises the foreigner and the eunuch a name better than sons and daughters, and Acts 8 records an African court official of the queen of the Ethiopians coming to faith. In the New Testament, Jesus is compared with Jeremiah, Matthew 16:14, speaks of Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets, Matthew 23:37, and the list of the faithful in Hebrews 11:36-38 includes those who endured chains and imprisonment.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer of these chapters, who stood close to Jeremiah, wanted the exiles to see that God's judgment on Jerusalem was not a failure of information or of opportunity. Zedekiah is shown at length precisely so that no one can say the king did not know. He sends to Jeremiah for a word, protects him from death, swears an oath in the LORD's name, and is told exactly what to do and what will happen if he does not. The story is built to put the cause of the fall where it belongs, in a man who knew what was right and did not do it.

It is also meant as a record of faithfulness at a price. Jeremiah does not change his message under pressure, and he does not soften it in the private room, where the king would have preferred a gentler word. The account gives the people in exile a prophet to be proud of and a pattern to follow: a man who spoke the word of the LORD in prison, in a mud pit and in a king's private chamber, and whose words were then borne out.

The writer also means to surprise. Hope enters the story from outside the circles of power, through a Cushite court official, who is the only person in the narrative who treats Jeremiah as a human being in danger. His brief speech to the king in 38:9 and his practical care in 38:11-12 stand as a rebuke to the insiders. By setting an outsider's courage against an insider's cowardice, the author keeps the focus where Jeremiah kept it: on who obeys, not on who belongs.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These chapters describe a siege, a prison and a king's failing, and they should not be turned into commands. Jeremiah's call to surrender was a specific word of the LORD for a specific city, 38:2, based on God's announced plan to give Judah into Babylon's hand, and it does not teach that believers must always yield to foreign powers or that resistance to tyranny is always wrong. Romans 13 and Acts 5:29 each have their own place in that wider discussion.

Jeremiah's reply to the officials in 38:26-27 describes what he did, which was to give them the true reason he had been to the king, and to keep back the rest at Zedekiah's request. The narrator neither praises nor blames him. It would be careless to take this as a general licence for half-truths whenever one is under pressure.

What does carry over is the shape of the choices. Fear of other people can override a conviction one holds in private, as it did with Zedekiah; courage can come from where it is least expected, as it did with Ebed-melech; and a person can obey God and suffer for it, and God does not leave him. The principle of Proverbs 29:25 is the standing application: 'The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.'

debates.question: Was Zedekiah a believer who simply lacked courage, or was his private interest in Jeremiah's words merely superstitious hedging?

views.label: A believer paralyzed by fear
views.case: Zedekiah protects Jeremiah's life more than once, seeks him out secretly and repeatedly, and swears an oath in the LORD's name, suggesting some genuine regard for the word even though fear of his officials keeps him from acting on it.

views.label: A man hedging his bets without real conviction
views.case: Zedekiah never once obeys the word he receives, continues to let his officials abuse Jeremiah, and asks Jeremiah to lie to protect him, patterns more consistent with using the prophet for information than genuinely submitting to God.

debates.bearing: Either reading warns that knowledge of God's word, even sought out sincerely and repeatedly, is not the same as obedience to it. 2 Chronicles 36:12 says plainly that he did not humble himself before Jeremiah.

debates.question: Was Jeremiah's call to surrender treason, as the officials charged?

views.label: Yes, a defeatist undermining the defence
views.case: The officials' charge in 38:4 is that he is discouraging the warriors and the people. In any siege, a voice that tells soldiers the cause is lost damages morale, and the Lachish letters show how seriously such talk was taken. From the standpoint of the city's defenders, he was working for the enemy.

views.label: No, a faithful prophet announcing God's verdict
views.case: Jeremiah did not act for Babylon. He spoke what the LORD had told him, as he had since 21:8-9, and he offered the city a way of life, 38:17. Ezekiel 17:13-16 shows that Zedekiah's real offence was breaking an oath sworn in God's name. Jeremiah's counsel was loyal to the people in the only way that could save them.

views.label: A fair charge from the outside, a false one from the inside
views.case: The officials were right that the message weakened resistance, and wrong about its motive. Jeremiah himself told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon, 29:7, which is the same concern for a people's good. Their claim that he seeks 'ruin' rather than well-being, 38:4, reverses his own language of shalom in 29:11.

debates.bearing: The chapter is built so that the reader sees the officials' accusation as the mirror image of the truth. The man charged with seeking the people's harm is the only one trying to save them.

debates.question: Did Jeremiah act rightly in telling the officials only part of what he and Zedekiah had said?

views.label: Yes, a justified withholding
views.case: The officials had no right to the king's private counsel, and Jeremiah's words in 38:26 were true: he had indeed presented a petition not to be returned to Jonathan's house, 37:20. Rahab is commended for welcoming the spies in peace, Hebrews 11:31, and God was good to the midwives who guarded the Hebrew boys, Exodus 1:17-21.

views.label: Doubtful, a compromise forced on a prophet
views.case: The narrative says that Jeremiah relayed 'the exact words the king had commanded him to say,' 38:27, which suggests he spoke as instructed rather than as he chose. His withholding served the king's fear rather than the LORD's word.

debates.bearing: The narrator reports the scene without comment. What we know is that Jeremiah told no lie, that the officials went away without the substance, and that his life was spared.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word is the mire itself. Jeremiah 38:6 says the cistern had no water but only mud, and 'Jeremiah sank down into the mud.' Both the noun, tit, and the verb, tava, belong to the language of the psalms of the drowning. Psalm 69:14 prays, 'Rescue me from the mire and do not let me sink,' and the pair of words is the same. The verb comes back in verse 22, in the poem the women will chant to the king: 'Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.' The prophet's feet sank in the mire in verse 6, and the king's are to sink in it in verse 22. The man who is carried out of the mud and the man who sinks into it are set against each other by a single word.

The second thing to notice is how the rescue is told. Ebed-melech is told to 'pull Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern,' verse 10, and in verse 13 'they pulled him up with the ropes.' The verb is the one for causing to go up, in the same stem. Psalm 40:2 uses it: 'He lifted me up from the pit of despair.' The psalmist's noun for the pit there is the same bor as in Jeremiah 38. A reader who knew the psalm would hear Jeremiah's rescue as an answer to its prayer.

In verses 17 and 18 the king is given the choice in a construction that repeats the verb. 'If you indeed surrender' reflects a Hebrew form in which the verb 'to go out' is doubled, which gives the sense 'if you will really go out.' The phrase is the language of coming out of a city to the besiegers, as Jehoiachin 'went out' to the king of Babylon, 2 Kings 24:12. For Zedekiah, to go out was to give up the city; and the word meant that he would be coming out of the place he thought was safe into a place that was actually safe.

The officials' accusation in verse 4 uses a vivid phrase that the BSB renders 'discouraging.' Literally, they say that Jeremiah is 'weakening the hands' of the warriors. The idiom is the one the Lachish letters use, a mark of how this charge was made in the ordinary speech of a besieged army. They also say Jeremiah seeks not shalom for this people but ra'ah, harm, which is the reverse of what God says of His own plans in Jeremiah 29:11.

The women's poem in verse 22 calls the friends who mislead the king 'trusted friends,' in Hebrew 'men of your shalom,' which is the term of Psalm 41:9, 'my close friend whom I trusted.' It is the word for the people who wish you well, and the poem says they were not.

Finally, the repeated 'hand' of verses 3, 5, 16, 18 and 19 carries the whole drama in a single noun. Everyone is delivered into someone's hand. In verse 5 the king says that Jeremiah is in the officials' hands, and in verse 16 he swears not to give Jeremiah into theirs. The word is the one by which Scripture speaks of power and protection alike.

typology.type: The prophet in the pit, Genesis 37:24
typology.fulfillment: Joseph, the dreamer sent by his father to his brothers, was thrown into a pit by his own family and drawn out by outsiders, and the pit became a step toward saving many lives, Genesis 50:20. Jeremiah's cistern repeats the shape: a righteous man cast down by his own people. Both stories find their greatest fulfilment in Christ, who was handed over by His own and 'delivered up' to the earth for three days, Matthew 12:40, and raised by the Father. The type falls short in that Joseph and Jeremiah were rescued from death while Christ went through death and out the other side, Acts 2:24.

Ebed-melech, a Cushite and perhaps a eunuch, is the one who defends God's prophet and attends to his comfort with rags for the ropes. His deed anticipates the words of Christ, 'I was in prison and you visited Me,' Matthew 25:36, and the way the gospel reaches the foreigner and the eunuch, as in the Ethiopian official of Acts 8:27-39, who is told the good news from Isaiah. Isaiah 56:3-5 promised that such people would not be shut out. The picture is limited: Ebed-melech saved a prophet's body, while Christ saves those who trust Him from death itself.

typology.type: The king who knows and yields, 38:5 and 38:19
typology.fulfillment: Zedekiah believes enough to protect Jeremiah in private and fears people too much to act in public, saying that the king 'can do nothing.' In John 18:38 Pilate says, 'I find no basis for a charge against Him,' and then, because the crowd shouts that he is no friend of Caesar, John 19:12, hands Jesus over, wishing to satisfy the crowd, Mark 15:15. The two scenes are a contrast rather than a prediction: the innocent person is brought before a ruler who sees the truth and surrenders it. Pilate's surrender led to the cross, where Zedekiah's led only to his own ruin.

Jeremiah is beaten, jailed and accused of seeking the people's ruin for telling them the way of life. Jesus draws the line Himself when He speaks of Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets, Matthew 23:37, and some of His contemporaries took Him for 'Jeremiah or one of the prophets,' Matthew 16:14. Hebrews lists those who endured chains and imprisonment, Hebrews 11:36-38. The escalation is that Jeremiah's word judged a city, while Christ's person is both the judgment and the rescue of it, Luke 19:41-44.

study.christ:
Jeremiah's story leads to Christ first as a pattern of the rejected prophet. Like Jeremiah, Jesus brought a message that the nation's leaders heard as a threat to the city. The charge against Jeremiah, that he sought the people's ruin and not their welfare, 38:4, has its echo in the accusation against Jesus that He stirred up the people and spoke against the temple. Jeremiah's question in 37:18, 'How have I sinned against you,' has its counterpart in Jesus' reply to the officer who struck Him, 'If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong,' John 18:23. Jesus could be mistaken in the minds of ordinary people for Jeremiah, Matthew 16:14, and He wept over Jerusalem as Jeremiah had, Luke 19:41-44, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace.'

It leads to Christ in the shape of the choice Jeremiah set before the king. 'Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine and plague, but whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live,' 38:2. That is the logic of a gospel that says that whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for Christ's sake will find it, Matthew 10:39. Jeremiah's surrender was to a foreign power and was a particular word for that city, so the parallel is one of shape and not of equation. But the shape is real: God sometimes calls His people to give up what they are holding to find the life they cannot keep. Hebrews 13:12-13 uses the idea of going out, saying that Jesus suffered outside the city gate and that we are to go out to Him outside the camp.

The pit also leads to Christ. Jeremiah's descent into the earth and his being brought up by the hands of others is a small picture of One who was laid in the earth and raised by the power of God. In Matthew 12:40 Jesus Himself takes up the story of a man swallowed and returned, and Peter says that God raised Jesus up, 'releasing Him from the agony of death,' Acts 2:24. The pit in Jeremiah 38 is not a prophecy of the tomb, and the narrator does not claim it as one. It is a pattern of the way God treats the faithful: He allows them to go down and does not leave them there.

Finally, there is Christ as the contrast to Zedekiah. The king who says that he can do nothing, 38:5, was in fact able to do everything and did nothing. The true King of Israel is the one who is able and does. He is also the true answer to Ebed-melech's rags and ropes: the one who comes down into the pit to lift others out, 'taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7.
study.god:
The chapters show a God whose word does not change when the audience becomes hostile. The message Jeremiah gives in prison in 37:17 is the same one he gave in the courtyard in 21:8-9 and gives again in the private room in 38:17: surrender and live. This consistency is itself an attribute of God. He is not worn down by refusal into a softer message, and He is not provoked into a harsher one. The truth stays the same, and the invitations keep coming.

They show a God who offers life even at the last. Verse 17 says that if the king surrenders, 'this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive.' This is startling, because Jeremiah has already said that the city will surely be given into Babylon's hand, 38:3, and 37:8 says that the Chaldeans will take it and burn it. Both are in the record. The announcement is God's settled intention, and the offer is His real invitation; and the chapter holds them together, as the book does elsewhere, 18:7-8. The way God speaks is to give people a true choice and to tell them honestly what each path leads to.

They show a God who works through people we would not choose. The prophet's life is not saved by the king, the priests, or the officials, but by a Cushite court official who is not even mentioned until the moment he is needed, and who has no standing to command the king. God's providence is not limited to the people who bear His name. Lamentations 3:56-57 gives the sufferer's view of such a rescue: 'You drew near when I called on You; You said, "Do not be afraid."'

They show God's patience with weakness. Zedekiah is no hero, yet the LORD continues to speak to him, sending for the prophet again and again. Some have seen in that a warning, since a person who is repeatedly offered life and refuses it hardens by the refusal. The book of Chronicles says Zedekiah 'stiffened his neck and hardened his heart,' 2 Chronicles 36:13.

For worship, the chapters teach us to bring our fears to the God who is able to keep what we cannot, and to ask Him to make us people who obey in the open what we believe in secret. They also remind us that the God who sent Jeremiah into the mud sent a man to pull him out.

crossReferences.note: Joseph is stripped and thrown into a pit by his brothers, and the narrator adds that it was empty. The setting, the betrayal by one's own, and the intervention of an outsider make the story of Joseph the oldest model for what happens to Jeremiah, though Jeremiah's pit holds mud.

A prayer from someone about to drown: 'Rescue me from the mire and do not let me sink.' The vocabulary of the mire and of sinking is the same as in Jeremiah 38:6 and 38:22, so the psalm reads like a prayer in Jeremiah's own mouth.

The answer to such a prayer: 'He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay.' Jeremiah is lifted out of a pit with the same verb, and the psalm helps the reader see that the rescue by Ebed-melech is also the LORD's doing.

A sufferer says he was dropped alive into a pit and that waters closed over his head, then that God drew near and said, 'Do not be afraid.' Whoever the speaker, the poem gives words to what Jeremiah's cistern meant, and shows what God does for the one in the pit.

The earlier statement of the same message to the same king's court, with the way of life and the way of death and the promise that whoever surrenders will retain his life like a spoil of war. The words of 38:2 are taken from this, so the officials were reacting to a message they had heard before.

God says His plans are for peace and a future, not for harm. In 38:4 the officials accuse Jeremiah of seeking the people's ruin and not their well-being, which turns God's own words about His plan upside down and gives the accusation its irony.

Ezekiel's account of Zedekiah's broken oath to Babylon, with the verdict that the king will die in Babylon, the land of the king who enthroned him. It shows what is at stake when Jeremiah tells him to surrender: the king's resistance is also a breach of covenant sworn in God's name.

A king imprisons the prophet Micaiah on bread and water for a word he did not want to hear. The scene is a precedent for Jeremiah's treatment, and for a king who prefers the prophets who say what he wants and punishes the one who tells the truth.

'The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.' A proverb that could serve as a summary of Zedekiah, who fears his officials and the defectors, 38:5 and 38:19, and in whom the snare is exactly what the proverb describes.

God promises the foreigner and the eunuch that they will not be excluded from His people, and that they will receive a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters. Ebed-melech, a Cushite and perhaps a eunuch, is a living instance of the promise, and Jeremiah 39:15-18 will give him his reward.

Jesus says that those who visited the prisoner and clothed the naked did it for Him. Ebed-melech's care for a prisoner with rags and ropes anticipates the kind of compassion Jesus names, and the lesson that mercy shown to God's servants is received as mercy to Himself.

Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, gave up the innocent Jesus to be crucified. Zedekiah's 'the king can do nothing to stop you,' Jeremiah 38:5, is the same kind of abdication by a ruler who knows better, and the two scenes warn about leaders who govern by what they fear.

study.oneStory:
From the Garden onwards the Bible is a story of God sending a word and of people deciding what to do with the messenger. Cain silences Abel, Joseph's brothers silence their brother in a pit, the prophets are stoned and jailed. Jeremiah in the cistern is one moment in that long history, and it is a moment in which the lines are drawn with unusual clarity: a king who knows the truth and will not obey it, officials who seek a quiet end to the voice that troubles them, and a prophet who will not take back a word.

Behind the scene lies the covenant at Sinai, whose terms the book of Deuteronomy spelled out: blessing for obedience, siege and exile for rebellion, Deuteronomy 28. By the time of Jeremiah 37 and 38 the curses of that covenant are arriving, and the only open question is whether the king will take the way out that God provides. The word of life is, as in the garden, a choice. 'I set before you the way of life and the way of death,' Jeremiah 21:8.

The story also keeps open the ancient hope that the outsider will find a place. From Rahab to Ruth to Naaman, from the Cushite in Jeremiah's court to the Ethiopian official who reads Isaiah on the road to Gaza, the people of God are repeatedly joined by those who were thought to be beyond its edges. Ebed-melech is a chapter in the story of how the promise to Abraham, that all nations will be blessed, begins to be kept even in Judah's darkest hour, Genesis 12:3.

The rejection of the prophet is carried to its end in Christ. He is the one who comes to Jerusalem with the word of life, who is handed over by rulers who know better, and who is laid in the earth and raised. In Him the logic of Jeremiah's cistern is finished: the one who goes down is brought up, and those who trust Him are brought up with Him. He is also the answer to the question of Jeremiah's day, whether God's word is able to save a people who have refused it.

The new creation completes the picture. In the city that is to come there is no siege, no famine, no prison and no cistern, and the gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25. The people of every nation bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:26, and the Cushite who helped a prophet out of the mud finds that his kindness was seen, and that the Lord who sees such things has made a home for him.

sermon.title: Christmas at the Castle, Part 5: Jeremiah 37-39
sermon.why: Carson works through the narrative of Jeremiah's arrest, imprisonment, and rescue from the cistern alongside Zedekiah's fearful, double minded response, tracing exactly the passage's own movement from chapter 37 through the fall of Jerusalem in chapter 39.

quiz.q: Why is Jeremiah first arrested at the Gate of Benjamin?

options.text: The captain of the guard falsely accuses him of deserting to the Chaldeans when he tries to leave the city on personal business.
options.note: Verses 12 to 14 record this false charge and Jeremiah's denial.

options.text: He is caught reading the burned scroll from the previous chapter.
options.note: That scroll incident belongs to chapter 36; his arrest here concerns a false desertion charge.

options.text: He publicly curses King Zedekiah in the marketplace.
options.note: The text records no public cursing; the charge is specifically desertion to the enemy.

options.text: He refuses to pray for the king when asked.
options.note: Jeremiah does pray and respond to Zedekiah's request; his arrest happens later, over the false desertion accusation.

quiz.q: What happens to Jeremiah in the cistern of Malchiah?

options.text: He is lowered by ropes into mud with no water, left to starve, then rescued by Ebed-melech the Cushite.
options.note: Verses 6 to 13 record both the intended slow death and the rescue.

options.text: He drowns in the water at the bottom of the cistern.
options.note: The text says the cistern had no water, only mud; he sinks into mud, not water.

options.text: He escapes on his own before anyone notices.
options.note: He is rescued by Ebed-melech's intervention and the king's men, not by his own escape.

options.text: King Zedekiah personally lowers him into the cistern.
options.note: It is the officials who do this, and Zedekiah says he cannot stop them, not that he did it himself.

quiz.q: Who rescues Jeremiah from the cistern, and how?

options.text: Ebed-melech the Cushite, who appeals to the king and then pulls Jeremiah out with ropes padded by old rags.
options.note: Verses 7 to 13 detail this rescue in full, including the padding to protect Jeremiah under his arms.

options.text: The prophet Jeremiah's own family members.
options.note: No family members appear in this rescue; it is Ebed-melech, a foreign court official.

options.text: King Zedekiah's officials who had originally thrown him in.
options.note: Those same officials wanted him dead; it is Ebed-melech who intervenes to save him instead.

options.text: The prophet Baruch, using a rope ladder.
options.note: Baruch does not appear in this rescue scene; Ebed-melech carries out the rescue with ropes and rags.

quiz.q: What does Zedekiah do after hearing Jeremiah's word in their final secret meeting?

options.text: He fears his own officials too much to surrender, and tells Jeremiah to hide the true content of their conversation.
options.note: Verses 19 and 24 to 27 show his fear of the officials and his instruction to conceal what was actually said.

options.text: He immediately surrenders to the Chaldeans as instructed.
options.note: He does the opposite; he never surrenders despite hearing the clear offer of life.

options.text: He has Jeremiah executed for treason.
options.note: Zedekiah protects Jeremiah's life throughout, even swearing an oath not to kill him.

options.text: He publicly announces Jeremiah's counsel to all the officials.
options.note: He does the opposite, insisting the conversation be kept secret from the officials.

quiz.q: What is the repeated offer Jeremiah gives Zedekiah throughout these two chapters?

options.text: Surrender to the Chaldeans and both the king and the city will live; refuse and the city will be burned and the king seized.
options.note: This exact offer appears in 38:17 to 18 and is consistent with Jeremiah's message throughout the siege.

options.text: Flee immediately to Egypt for safety.
options.note: Jeremiah never counsels flight to Egypt here; that theme appears later, after Jerusalem's fall.

options.text: Gather an army and fight the Chaldeans directly.
options.note: Jeremiah's consistent counsel is surrender, not armed resistance.

options.text: Offer sacrifices in the temple to appease the LORD's anger.
options.note: The offer is specifically political surrender to Babylon, not a call to ritual sacrifice.

questions: Zedekiah sought God's word repeatedly and privately believed enough of it to protect Jeremiah's life, yet fear of his officials kept him from ever obeying it. Where does fear of what others will think keep you from acting on what you already know is true?

Ebed-melech, an outsider with no political stake in the outcome, was the one person in the palace who acted to save God's prophet. Where might God be calling you to act with costly courage even though it is not officially your responsibility?

Jeremiah told the truth at real personal cost, beaten and nearly left to die for it, yet never stopped repeating the same offer of life. What would it look like for you to keep speaking a hard truth in love even when it is not welcomed?

God preserved Jeremiah's life through mud and imprisonment, not by removing the suffering but by sustaining him through it. Where do you need to trust God's preserving care in a hard season rather than expecting Him to remove the hardship altogether?
Zedekiah asked for the truth secretly but wanted to manage how it was known publicly. Where are you tempted to seek God's counsel privately while avoiding the public cost of actually living it out?

translationNotes.note: To claim his portion likely refers to a family land transaction or inheritance matter in Benjamin, an ordinary personal errand that Irijah's suspicion twisted into a capital charge of desertion.

The cistern of Malchiah having no water but only mud explains why Jeremiah does not simply drown, and also why the officials could claim they had not directly executed him, a slower and more deniable form of killing.

Zedekiah's fear is specifically of Judean deserters already among the Chaldeans, not of the Chaldeans themselves, revealing his fear of local political retribution and mockery rather than the invading army.
